items.title: Mary I burned around 280 Protestants
items.claim: Mary I's reign (1553-1558) earned the 'Bloody Mary' epithet through executions. How many died?

options.text: Around 10,000 — comparable to Henry VIII's executions
Around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, plus 30 who died in prison — a smaller toll than Henry VIII's or Elizabeth I's overall execution numbers
Over 50,000 in a state campaign of terror
No confirmed executions for religion — the epithet is entirely myth

items.reveal:
John Foxe's 'Actes and Monuments' (1563, later 'Foxe's Book of Martyrs') chronicled the Marian burnings in vivid detail and became a foundational Protestant text. Henry VIII executed an estimated 57,000 (Holinshed's figure, contested) including thousands of vagrants; Elizabeth I executed around 200 Catholic priests and Jesuits.

Mary's numbers were lower in absolute terms but concentrated (1555-1558) and ideological. The propaganda effect outlasted the regime.
items.why: Reputation is unevenly distributed. Mary's image as uniquely cruel says more about the durability of Protestant propaganda than about Tudor execution rates.

items.title: Henry VII was a 'modern' monarch — by destroying the nobility
items.claim: How did Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) consolidate power?

options.text: By distributing land widely among loyal nobles
By using bonds and recognisances to financially bind nobles, the Star Chamber to bypass juries, and avoiding war to keep crown finances strong
By creating a standing army of 50,000 men
By moving the capital from London to York

items.reveal:
Henry VII forced nobles to enter bonds — written debts payable to the crown on bad behaviour. By 1509 around two-thirds of the peerage was under bond. Empson and Dudley managed crown revenue ruthlessly.

The Star Chamber, sitting at Westminster, dealt with cases the common-law courts could not — overmighty nobles intimidating juries. Henry VII left £1.5 million in the treasury (his son spent it in a decade). He fought one continental war.
items.why: Henry VII is the boring Tudor — but his fiscal-administrative state is what makes Henry VIII's ambition possible. Modern bureaucratic monarchy starts here, not at the Reformation.

items.title: Charles I lost the Civil War partly because he was a poor commander
items.claim: What contributed to Charles I's defeat (1642-1646) beyond political 'tyranny'?

options.text: Parliamentary forces always vastly outnumbered the king's

Parliament held London (wealth, manpower), the navy, and after 1645 the New Model Army; Charles repeatedly failed to coordinate his commanders and missed strategic opportunities like marching on London after Edgehill
The Scots refused to fight on either side
Charles was killed in battle at Naseby

items.reveal_title: The man, not just the cause
items.reveal:
After the indecisive Edgehill (October 1642), Charles failed to march on London while it was undefended. The Solemn League and Covenant (1643) brought Scottish forces in on Parliament's side. The New Model Army (formed 1645) under Fairfax and Cromwell was the first national professional army.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646; they handed him to Parliament. His attempts to negotiate while plotting a second war (the 'Engagement' with the Scots, 1647) destroyed any remaining trust and led to his trial.
items.why: Wars are won by armies, logistics and leadership — not just by who has the better political argument. Charles's strategic failures are often glossed over in the rush to debate 'tyranny vs liberty'.
